passage: Since the argument with his manager on Monday, Bao's mind had been looping every evening in his London flat: what he should have said, what she'd think of him, whether he'd be let go. On Thursday he caught himself mid-loop in the kitchen and tried what his flatmate Kwame had suggested. He wrote the thought on a sticky note: "Worried she thinks I'm difficult." He set a timer for fifteen minutes and let himself think about it properly, even jotting one thing he could say to her on Friday. When the timer rang, he stuck the note on the fridge and started cooking pho from scratch: chopping, stirring, tasting. By the time the broth was ready, his head was quiet. Kwame, tasting it, said, "If the loops ever get constant or really dark, talk to someone professional, yeah?" Bao nodded. "I will."

qa.q: What did Bao write on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Worried she thinks I'm difficult."

qa.q: Why did the looping feel hard for Bao to stop on his own?
qa.a: He was worried about his job and his manager's opinion, so going over it felt necessary, as if the next replay might settle it.

qa.q: Which steps helped Bao break the loop that evening?
qa.a: Writing the thought down, giving it fifteen timed minutes with one action for Friday, then cooking something absorbing.

qa.q: Why might Kwame mention talking to a professional?
qa.a: Kwame cares about Bao and knows that if the loops become constant or dark, a trained person can help more than tricks alone.

grounding: An adult notices rumination, writes the thought down, gives it a set time, then cooks, with a friend noting when to seek professional help.

passage: At the software firm in Chennai, Karthik booked a slot with Sabina, the in-house counsellor, after two weeks of replaying a failed product demo every night. "I lie there going over it," he said. "What went wrong, what they think of me. It never ends." Sabina nodded. "Let's try something. When it starts, write the thought down, word for word. Give it fifteen minutes, a real appointment, at seven. Then do something that needs your hands and head, like cooking or a walk." She added, "And if the thoughts start coming all the time, or turn really dark, come back to me straight away or see a doctor. That's important." That evening at seven Karthik wrote, "I embarrassed myself in front of the client." He thought about it for fifteen minutes, then went for a brisk walk round the lake. He was asleep by eleven.

qa.q: What did Karthik write at seven that evening?
qa.a: "I embarrassed myself in front of the client."

qa.q: Why had the replaying felt endless to Karthik?
qa.a: Karthik felt embarrassed about the demo and kept trying to work out what went wrong and what the client thought, and with no set limit the thoughts circled every night.

qa.q: Which parts of Sabina's plan helped Karthik sleep?
qa.a: Writing the thought down, giving it a fixed fifteen-minute slot, then taking a brisk walk, so the worry had a place and an end.

qa.q: Why does Sabina stress coming back if the thoughts become constant or dark?
qa.a: Sabina wants Karthik to know the simple routine has limits, and that ongoing or dark thoughts deserve professional help straight away.

grounding: A counsellor teaches an adult to write the thought down, time-box it and then do something absorbing, with a note on when to seek help.

Dear Kalyani,
You asked how I'm doing since the shop closed. Honestly, the first weeks were bad. I kept going over it at night: the rent, the loan, what everyone in the para must be saying. My mind wouldn't stop. So I tried something a doctor friend suggested. When the loop starts, I write the thought in a small notebook, exactly as it sounds in my head. Then I give it twenty minutes, sitting at the table after dinner, to think it through properly. When the time's up, I close the notebook and do something with my hands. Mostly I cook. Last night I made your favourite shorshe ilish, badly. It helps. Not every night, but most. And I promised Ma that if it gets constant or very dark, I'll go and see someone properly. I will.
Your brother,
Arnab

qa.a: Twenty minutes, sitting at the table after dinner.

qa.q: Why were the first weeks after the shop closed so hard for Arnab?
qa.a: Worry about the rent, the loan and what people were saying kept circling at night, and going over it felt necessary but brought no rest.

qa.q: Which steps from the letter could someone else try?

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel reading this letter?

grounding: An adult breaks nightly rumination by writing thoughts down, time-boxing them and cooking, and promises to seek help if it worsens.

You asked how I got through the month after the pitch, Aditi. Honestly? Badly at first. Every night I'd lie there replaying what the investor said, that my plan was "charming but naive." Round and round till two.
Then my cousin, who's a counsellor, told me something simple: "Zainab, when it starts, catch it." So now I keep a notebook by the stove. I write the thought exactly: "They think I'm naive." I set my phone timer for ten minutes and let myself chew on it properly. When it rings, I close the book and start cooking, something fiddly, like rolling parathas or doing biryani from scratch. My hands get busy, and my head follows.
Some nights it still comes back. But my cousin also said that if it ever stops lifting, or gets really dark, I should see someone properly. I've kept that promise to myself.

qa.a: Zainab keeps a notebook by the stove.

qa.a: Zainab felt hurt and belittled by 'charming but naive', which seemed like a verdict on Zainab, so replaying it felt like trying to answer it and kept Zainab awake till two.

I'm Nazia, and I share a flat with Bidisha in Salt Lake. Since her project was handed to someone else at work, I've seen a pattern at night. She'd sit on the sofa staring at the switched-off TV, and when I asked, she'd say, "Just thinking about the meeting again."
Last week something changed. Around nine she took out a small yellow pad, wrote a line I couldn't see, and put her phone on the table with a timer running. She sat with the pad till it beeped. Then she stood up, tied her hair back and said, "Walk?" We did two rounds of the park by the lake. Another night she made shukto from her mother's recipe, humming.
I can't say what's in her head now. But she laughs at dinner again. And I've told her that if it ever gets constant or dark, I'll go with her to a counsellor.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say when Nazia asked about the staring?
qa.a: She'd say, "Just thinking about the meeting again."

qa.q: Why can't Nazia be sure how Bidisha feels now, and what hints are there?
qa.a: Nazia only sees the outside and couldn't read the yellow pad, but the walks, the humming while cooking and the laughter at dinner suggest her evenings feel lighter.

qa.q: Which part of Bidisha's new evening seems to break the loop, and why?
qa.a: Stopping when the timer beeps and moving straight into a walk or cooking shukto gives the thought a set time and then something absorbing to fill the mind.

qa.q: How has Bidisha's change affected Nazia?
qa.a: Nazia no longer comes home to someone staring at a blank TV and can share walks and dinners again, while staying ready to go with Bidisha to a counsellor if things get worse.

grounding: A flatmate observes an adult who writes the looping thought down, gives it a timed slot and then walks or cooks, with a counsellor in mind if it becomes constant or dark.

Monday. Francis's presentation to the board had gone badly. By night he had replayed it fifty times: the slide that froze, the director's frown. He noticed his jaw was clenched and he'd been lying awake for an hour. He got up, wrote on a notepad: "I worry the board thinks I'm incompetent." Then he set a timer for fifteen minutes and let himself think about it. When the timer rang, he closed the pad and went back to bed.

Wednesday. The thoughts came again at dinner. Francis wrote them down, gave them ten minutes, then went out and walked around the lake with his friend Nitin. "Doing better?" Nitin asked. "A bit." "If it keeps being this heavy, you know you can talk to someone, right?" "I know. I'll see how it goes."

Saturday. Francis cooked a slow biryani for friends. He noticed he hadn't thought about the presentation all day.

passage: Yash, you say you can't stop thinking about the breakup? Let me tell you what I learned at twenty-four, as a young woman whose engagement had just broken. For months I lay awake going over every conversation. What did I do wrong? What if I'd said something different? I thought I was understanding it. I was only sinking. One day my college friend, a doctor now, said, "Gopika, write it down. Give it fifteen minutes a day, not twenty-four hours." So every evening I wrote in a notebook for fifteen minutes. Then I closed it and made rotis, slowly, the whole batch. It sounds silly. But my hands were busy and my head got quiet. Some days it was still very dark. On those days I went to a counsellor at the hospital. Both helped. So, Yash, the notebook, the rotis, and the counsellor if it's too heavy.

qa.q: What did young Gopika make after closing the notebook each evening?
qa.a: Rotis, the whole batch.

qa.q: How did young Gopika feel lying awake going over every conversation?
qa.a: She felt like she was sinking, low and stuck, even though it felt like understanding.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Gopika break the loop?

qa.q: How might Gopika's doctor friend have felt seeing her so stuck?

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how writing thoughts down, limiting the time for them and doing something absorbing helped, with professional help on dark days.

passage: The night shift at the Pune hospital ended at seven, but Sarita's mind kept going. A patient's son had shouted at her that morning, accusing her of ignoring his father. She hadn't, but she replayed it on the bus, at breakfast, in bed. By noon she still couldn't sleep. She sat up, took her diary, and wrote: "I'm afraid I let that family down." Then she set her phone timer for ten minutes and thought about it on purpose. When the timer rang, she put on her shoes and walked to the market for vegetables, choosing tomatoes carefully. At home she slept for five hours. That evening she told her friend Pallavi. "It keeps coming back." "If it stays this heavy, the hospital has a staff counsellor," Pallavi said. "I know," Sarita said. "I'll book it if it doesn't ease this week."

qa.q: What did Sarita write in her diary?
qa.a: "I'm afraid I let that family down."

qa.q: Why did Sarita struggle to sleep after the shift?
qa.a: She felt upset and anxious, replaying the son's accusation even though she hadn't ignored his father.

qa.q: What did Sarita do to break the loop, and what is her back-up plan?
qa.a: She wrote the thought down, gave it ten minutes, then did something absorbing like shopping; if it stays heavy she plans to see the staff counsellor.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel hearing that the thoughts keep coming back?

grounding: It shows an adult who notices she is ruminating, writes the thought down, sets a short time for it and does something absorbing, with professional help if it continues.

Mahima caught herself in the shower on Saturday morning, arguing with her sister again in her head about the words at Friday's dinner. She'd had the same argument at midnight, and at three.

She got out, dried her hair and took the small green notebook off the fridge. She wrote: "I'm still hurt about what Madhav said about my job." Then she set the kitchen timer for ten minutes and let herself think about it properly, pen moving.

When the timer rang she closed the notebook. The thought tugged at her. She tied on an apron and started kneading dough for parathas, slowly, feeling the flour under her nails. By the third paratha she was humming.

At lunch she told her flatmate about the notebook. "And if it ever starts running all day or getting dark," she added, "I've promised myself I'll book a counsellor."

qa.a: Mahima set the kitchen timer for ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Mahima feel she needed to stop the argument in her head?

"You're doing the thing again," Ayesha said, poking Tejas's arm on the sofa.

"What thing?"

"The staring thing. Is it the interview?"

"I keep replaying the answer about my weaknesses. I sounded like a robot."

"How many times today?"

"Maybe thirty."

"Okay. Remember what you tried last month?"

Tejas sighed, got up and fetched the notepad. He wrote: 'Robot answer. Might cost me the job.' "Fifteen minutes," he said, setting his phone timer.

"I'll be in the kitchen."

He wrote more, crossed some out, wrote a better answer for next time. When the timer beeped, he put the pen down.

"Done?"

"Done for today. Walk?"

"Walk."

On the stairs he said, "If it gets like last winter again, I'll call that therapist."

"Good," Ayesha said, and squeezed his hand.

qa.a: Tejas set the phone timer for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling as he replayed the interview answer?
qa.a: Tejas felt embarrassed and worried, sure he had sounded like a robot and that it might cost him the job.

qa.q: How did Ayesha support Tejas without taking over?
qa.a: Ayesha named the pattern, reminded him of his own method and gave him space in the kitchen, then joined the walk.

qa.q: How does Ayesha likely feel when Tejas mentions the therapist?

passage:
I'm Ankita, and I used to think turning a problem over all night was being responsible.

Last month my landlord raised the rent and I spent evenings running the same sums in my head, lying on the floor with the fan clicking. I'd get up exhausted.

My friend Rafiq showed me what he does. Now when I catch the loop, I write the worry in one line on a card. I give it twenty minutes at the table with tea, no phone. I actually think: options, costs, who to ask. When the twenty minutes end, I cook something fiddly. Last night it was dosa batter. Grinding it takes all my attention.

It doesn't vanish. But it shrinks. And Rafiq made me promise something too: if it ever gets constant, or dark, I don't try to handle it with cards. I see someone qualified. I've kept a counsellor's number on the fridge, just in case.

qa.q: What did Ankita cook last night?
qa.a: Last night it was dosa batter.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel back when the sums ran all night?
qa.a: Ankita felt exhausted and trapped in the loop, yet at the time thought turning it over was being responsible.

qa.q: Why does cooking something fiddly help Ankita after the twenty minutes?
qa.a: It takes Ankita's full attention, so the mind has somewhere else to go once the set worry time ends.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel about Ankita's counsellor number on the fridge?
qa.a: Rafiq would probably feel relieved and glad Ankita took the promise seriously, knowing help is ready if the thoughts turn constant or dark.

grounding: An adult describes writing worries down, giving them set time, cooking something absorbing, and keeping professional help ready.

Counsellor's session note — Bhavna
Yamini, 25, came back for her second session. Last time she described lying awake replaying a tense conversation with her manager, sometimes for hours.
This week she tried the plan we made. When she noticed the replay starting, she wrote the thought on a notepad by her bed: Manager thinks I'm careless. Then she gave it a slot: fifteen minutes the next evening at seven, at the dining table, to think it through. After writing, she got up and did something absorbing. Twice it was cooking dal from scratch; once it was a walk around the colony.
She said the thoughts came back, but "they had somewhere to go." In the seven o'clock slot, she noticed half of them already felt smaller.
I reminded her that if the thoughts become constant, or turn dark, she should tell me straight away or call the helpline number I gave her. We meet again in two weeks.

qa.q: What did Yamini write on the notepad by her bed?
qa.a: She wrote, "Manager thinks I'm careless."

qa.q: How did Yamini feel about the thoughts after trying the plan?
qa.a: She felt more in control and a bit relieved; the thoughts still came, but they "had somewhere to go" and felt smaller by the evening slot.

qa.q: Why does the three-step plan help with rumination?
qa.a: Writing the thought down and giving it a set time stops it taking over the night, and an absorbing task like cooking pulls attention away from the replay.

qa.q: How might Yamini's manager be affected if Yamini sleeps better?
qa.a: The manager may notice a more rested, focused Yamini at work, without knowing about the replays at night.

grounding: It shows, through a counsellor's note, an adult noticing rumination, writing the thought down, giving it a set time and turning to cooking or walking, with professional help if it turns constant or dark.

Tuesday night
New trick, day five. I'm Reena, and I've been a champion overthinker since school.
This week's loop: the presentation where my slides froze. I'd been replaying it at the office, on the metro, in the shower.
My friend Mehak, who went through something similar, told me what her counsellor taught her. When you notice the loop, write the thought down in one line. Give it a time slot, like fifteen minutes after dinner. Then do something that needs your hands and eyes.
So tonight I wrote: Everyone thinks I'm unprofessional. Then I made rotis, properly, rolling each one round. By the time I finished, the thought had shrunk. At 9:30, in my slot, I looked at the line again. It looked dramatic on paper.
Mehak also said if it ever gets constant or dark, go see someone. I've saved the number, just in case.

qa.a: Reena felt calmer, noticing the thought had shrunk and even looked dramatic on paper.

The flour mill in Alka's small town shut at five, and by six the argument with her supervisor was playing in her head for the tenth time. She was sitting on the back step, not shelling the peas she'd bought.
She knew this feeling. She took the notebook from the kitchen shelf and wrote it out: He said I was careless in front of everyone. I think he was unfair. I'll think about it properly tomorrow, 7 pm, fifteen minutes.
Then she closed the book, washed the peas and started the pulao, stirring onions until they turned gold. Her mind went back once; she let it pass and chopped the coriander.
When Nazia came over later, Alka said, "It still bothers me." Nazia nodded. "If it ever starts following you all day, or gets dark, talk to someone trained, okay?" Alka agreed.
